stem: A hospitalized client has an indwelling urinary catheter. Which nursing plan best aligns with current CDC CAUTI-prevention guidance?

options.A: Verify that a valid indication remains, maintain an intact closed drainage system with unobstructed flow, and remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.
options.B: Disconnect the drainage tubing daily for routine cleaning and reconnect it after the tubing has air-dried.
options.C: Continue the catheter for staff convenience when the client is incontinent even if no other clinical indication remains.
options.D: Use routine systemic antibiotics and antiseptic meatal cleaning while the catheter remains in place to prevent bacteriuria.

rationale: A is correct. CDC recommends inserting urinary catheters only for appropriate indications, leaving them in place only as long as needed, maintaining a closed drainage system after aseptic insertion, keeping urine flow unobstructed, and using quality-improvement processes such as daily review to identify catheters that can be removed. B breaks the closed system without a clinical indication. C is specifically listed as inappropriate catheter use when the catheter substitutes for incontinence care. D is incorrect because CDC does not recommend routine systemic antimicrobials for CAUTI prevention and recommends routine hygiene rather than antiseptic periurethral cleaning while the catheter is in place.
educational_objective: Prevent CAUTI by limiting indwelling catheter use to valid indications, maintaining a continuously closed and unobstructed drainage system, and reassessing daily for prompt removal rather than using routine antimicrobial prophylaxis or unnecessary system disconnections.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Clinical Safety: Preventing Catheter-associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTIs); Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections — Summary of Recommendations
source_version_date: Clinical Safety page dated June 27, 2025; CAUTI guideline web pages current through 2024; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Clinical Safety recommendations: use urinary catheters only when needed, place using aseptic technique/sterile equipment, maintain the closed sterile drainage system, and remove as soon as no longer needed. Summary of Recommendations I.A: insert only for appropriate indications and leave only as long as needed; III.A and III.B: maintain a closed drainage system and unobstructed urine flow; III.F and III.G: do not routinely use systemic antimicrobials or antiseptic periurethral cleaning for CAUTI prevention; IV.A: use QI strategies including daily review of continued need and removal of unnecessary catheters.
source_claim_supported: CAUTI prevention requires appropriate catheter indication, aseptic insertion, maintenance of a closed unobstructed drainage system, and prompt removal when no longer needed; routine antimicrobial prophylaxis and antiseptic meatal cleaning are not recommended.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: use aseptic technique, maintain invasive devices safely, and implement measures to prevent healthcare-associated infection.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — CAUTI prevention
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw bundle-recall item into a bedside catheter-management plan anchored to CDC's exact current recommendations. Added realistic errors involving unnecessary disconnection, convenience catheterization, prophylactic antibiotics, and antiseptic meatal care.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against current CDC Clinical Safety CAUTI guidance and the CDC Summary of Recommendations.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A combines four supported prevention elements. B intentionally violates closed-system maintenance. C is an explicit inappropriate-use example. D contradicts CDC recommendations against routine prophylactic antimicrobials and antiseptic meatal cleaning.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; indication, closed system, unobstructed flow, prompt removal.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; routine disconnection compromises the closed system.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; staff convenience/incontinence alone is not an appropriate indication.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; routine antibiotics and antiseptic periurethral cleaning are not recommended for CAUTI prevention.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A is fully concordant with the CDC prevention framework.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are concrete catheter-management plans.
audit_findings.blueprint: Prevention of device-associated infection directly maps to Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked closed-system exceptions, routine hygiene, prophylactic antimicrobial guidance, and indication/removal language. No unsupported universal timing or second answer remained.
